related_questions.question: At what age is Addison's disease usually diagnosed?

text_blocks.snippet: Addison's disease, also known as primary adrenal insufficiency, is most commonly diagnosed in adults between the ages of 30 and 50. While it can affect individuals of any age, it's less frequent in children and young adults. In rare cases, it can be inherited and present in childhood or adolescence.

list.title: Typical Age of Diagnosis:
list.snippet: The majority of Addison's disease cases are diagnosed in adults between 30 and 50 years old.

list.title: Can Occur at Any Age:
list.snippet: While the peak age range is 30-50, Addison's disease can occur at any age, including childhood and older adulthood.

list.title: Inherited Form:
list.snippet: In rare instances, Addison's disease is inherited and can manifest in childhood or adolescence.

list.title: Factors Increasing Risk:
list.snippet: Individuals with other autoimmune conditions, like Type 1 diabetes, are at a higher risk of developing Addison's disease.

list.title: Gender Differences:
list.snippet: Addison's disease is slightly more common in women than men, though the reasons are not fully understood.

related_questions.question: What does Addison's disease look like?

text_blocks.snippet: Addison's disease, also known as adrenal insufficiency, is characterized by a range of symptoms, most notably skin changes, fatigue, and low blood pressure. Hyperpigmentation (darkening of the skin) is a key indicator, particularly in sun-exposed areas and pressure points. Other common symptoms include fatigue, weakness, weight loss, and digestive issues like nausea and vomiting.
snippet_highlighted_words: skin changes, fatigue, and low blood pressure

list.title: Hyperpigmentation:
list.snippet: Darkening of the skin, especially in sun-exposed areas (face, forehead, shoulders), and in creases like those on the palms, elbows, and knuckles.

list.title: Black freckles:
list.snippet: Darker and more noticeable freckles than normal, particularly in people with fair skin.

list.title: Vitiligo:
list.snippet: White patches on the skin, which may occur in addition to hyperpigmentation.
Fatigue and Weakness: Persistent tiredness and a lack of energy, which can be debilitating.
Low Blood Pressure: Especially when standing up, causing dizziness and fainting.
Weight Loss: Unexplained weight loss due to decreased appetite.
Digestive Issues: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Salt Cravings: Intense desire for salty foods.
Hair Loss: In some cases, hair loss in the armpits and pubic area.
Adrenal Crisis: If left untreated, Addison's disease can lead to a life-threatening adrenal crisis with symptoms like severe dehydration, pale skin, rapid breathing, and loss of consciousness.
Autoimmune Reaction: In most cases, Addison's disease is caused by the body's immune system attacking the adrenal glands.
Infections: Certain infections can damage the adrenal glands.
Tumors: Tumors in the adrenal glands or pituitary gland can also cause Addison's disease.

list.title: Blood Tests:
list.snippet: Blood tests can measure hormone levels and identify antibodies associated with autoimmune Addison's disease.

list.title: ACTH Stimulation Test:
list.snippet: This test assesses how well the adrenal glands respond to ACTH, a hormone that stimulates cortisol production.

list.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy:
list.snippet: Lifelong hormone replacement therapy with glucocorticoids (like hydrocortisone or prednisone) and mineralocorticoids (like fludrocortisone) is the primary treatment.

list.title: Managing Adrenal Crisis:
list.snippet: Individuals with Addison's disease need to be prepared for potential adrenal crises and have a plan for emergency treatment.

text_blocks.snippet: Addison's disease, also known as adrenal insufficiency, is a condition where the adrenal glands don't produce enough cortisol and aldosterone, which are vital for managing stress, blood pressure, and other bodily functions. In children, it's often caused by an autoimmune reaction where the body's immune system attacks the adrenal glands. Symptoms can be mild initially, especially when the child is under physical stress, and may include fatigue, weakness, and low blood pressure. If left untreated, it can lead to serious complications like adrenal crisis, characterized by severe weakness, kidney failure, and shock.
snippet_highlighted_words: often caused by an autoimmune reaction where the body's immune system attacks the adrenal glands

text_blocks.snippet: Key aspects of Addison's disease in children:

list.title: Causes:
list.snippet: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands is the most common cause in developed countries. Other potential causes include genetic conditions, infections, bleeding, and tumors.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Early symptoms can be subtle, including fatigue, weakness, weight loss, and salt cravings. In children, slow weight gain can also be a sign. Severe symptoms, such as vomiting, diarrhea, and low blood pressure, can occur during periods of physical stress, illness, or injury.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Diagnosis involves blood tests to measure cortisol and ACTH levels, as well as ACTH stimulation tests to assess the adrenal gland's response. CT scans may be used to evaluate the adrenal glands for any abnormalities.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Addison's disease requires lifelong hormone replacement therapy, typically with corticosteroids and sometimes mineralocorticoids, to replace the missing hormones. In times of stress, higher doses of medication may be needed.

list.title: Adrenal Crisis:
list.snippet: A severe, life-threatening complication of Addison's disease, characterized by low blood pressure, low blood sugar, and dehydration. Immediate medical attention is crucial during an adrenal crisis.

list.title: Living with Addison's:
list.snippet: Children with Addison's disease need to be closely monitored by their healthcare provider, and parents need to be educated about recognizing and managing symptoms, especially during illness or stress.
